intro: This branch introduces the integral, which adds up many tiny pieces to find a total, such as distance from speed or area under a curve. It ends with the key link showing integrals undo derivatives.

VI.4.01.what: Finding a total by measuring area under a graph. For example, the area under a speed graph gives the distance traveled.

levels.a: Finds distance traveled from the area under a velocity graph.
levels.b: Explains that rate times time appears as an area on a graph.
levels.c: Treats area below the axis as negative, like driving backwards.
levels.d: Works out the units of area under a curve, such as meters.

VI.4.02.what: Estimating area under a curve by filling it with rectangles, using the left or right edge to set each height.

levels.a: Divides the area into rectangles and adds up their areas.
levels.b: Uses the curve's height at each left edge for the rectangles.
levels.c: Uses the curve's height at each right edge instead.
levels.d: Decides whether the estimate is too high or too low.

VI.4.03.what: Better area estimates using the middle of each strip, or using slanted-top strips (trapezoids).

levels.a: Estimates area using rectangles set at each strip's midpoint.
levels.b: Estimates area using trapezoids instead of rectangles.
levels.c: Makes these estimates from a table of values.

VI.4.04.what: Getting the exact area by using more and more thinner rectangles, and taking the limit as their number grows without end.

levels.a: Writes a rectangle sum using sigma (summation) notation.
levels.b: Writes the width of each strip and where each one sits.
levels.c: Takes the limit as the number of strips grows endlessly.
levels.d: Converts such a limit of sums into integral notation.

VI.4.05.what: How an integral is written and read: the start and end points, the function, and the "dx" marking thin strips.

levels.a: Identifies the start and end points and the function in an integral.
levels.b: Explains "dx" as the tiny width of each strip.
levels.d: Interprets an integral as area, with below-axis parts counting as negative.

VI.4.06.what: Rules for working with integrals, such as splitting them into pieces or flipping the start and end.

levels.a: Knows that swapping start and end points flips the sign.
levels.b: Splits an integral over a stretch into two neighboring stretches.
levels.c: Pulls out constants and splits up sums.
levels.d: Compares integrals: a bigger function gives a bigger integral.

VI.4.07.what: Finding integrals exactly using familiar shapes like triangles and semicircles, without any calculus rules.

levels.a: Finds integrals from areas of triangles and rectangles.
levels.b: Uses semicircle areas for circular graphs.
levels.d: Uses symmetry, where equal areas above and below cancel out.

VI.4.08.what: An antiderivative undoes a derivative: given the rate, it recovers the original function.

levels.a: Finds a function whose derivative is the given one.
levels.b: Adds "plus C", since any constant could have been there.
levels.c: Sees the answers as a family of curves stacked vertically.
levels.d: Checks an antiderivative by differentiating it.

VI.4.09.what: The basic rules for finding antiderivatives, starting with running the power rule backwards.

levels.a: Uses the power rule in reverse: raise the power by one and divide.
levels.c: Knows one over x comes from the natural log.
levels.d: Rewrites roots and fractions as powers before finding antiderivatives.

VI.4.10.what: Antiderivatives of trigonometry and exponential functions, found by reversing their derivative rules.

levels.a: Finds antiderivatives of sine and cosine.
levels.b: Finds antiderivatives of secant squared and secant times tangent.
levels.c: Finds antiderivatives of e to the x and other exponentials.
levels.d: Recognizes forms whose antiderivatives are inverse trig functions.

VI.4.11.what: Recovering a specific function from its rate of change plus one known value, like finding position from speed and a starting point.

levels.a: Finds the general antiderivative with its "plus C".
levels.b: Uses one known point to pin down the value of C.
levels.c: Finds position from velocity and a starting position.
levels.d: Works back twice, from acceleration to velocity to position.

VI.4.12.what: The first part of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: the rate at which area builds up equals the height of the curve.

levels.a: Differentiates an integral whose end point is x.
levels.b: Combines this with the chain rule when the end point is a formula.
levels.c: Handles integrals where the start point is variable.
levels.d: Handles integrals where both start and end are variable.

VI.4.13.what: The second part of the Fundamental Theorem: to find an exact area, take any antiderivative and subtract its values at the two ends.

levels.a: Writes the result as the antiderivative at the end minus at the start.
levels.b: Evaluates definite integrals using this method.
levels.c: Explains why this shortcut gives the area.
levels.d: Applies it to functions defined in pieces.

VI.4.14.what: A running total function that tracks how much area has piled up from a starting point to x.

levels.a: Defines a running total as an integral with a variable end point.
levels.b: Finds values of the running total from a graph.
levels.c: Finds where the running total increases.
levels.d: Finds its peaks, valleys and bends from the original graph.

VI.4.15.what: The average height of a curve over a stretch, like the average temperature across a whole day.

levels.a: States the formula: the integral divided by the stretch's length.
levels.b: Computes the average value of a function.
levels.c: Finds where the function actually hits its average value.
levels.d: Interprets the average value in a real-world setting.
